### case-study--deniskin-depth-jumps-after-resistance-and-rest-as-a-training-means.md
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: case-study
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "5.3"
     7	topic: depth jumps after resistance block
     8	category: [plyometrics, sequencing, recovery, explosive-strength, weightlifting]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Deniskin (1976): A Resistance Stage, Then Two Depth-Jump Stages, With Complete Rest Between Them
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "qualified athletes modelled different variants of weightlifting pre-competition training under laboratory conditions (Deniskin, 1976)." The test movement was "A leg extension movement involving the lifting of a 1RM ... starting with an initial knee angle of 90°." Stage 1 was "intensive work with resistance, the purpose of which was to increase explosive strength." "Only depth-jumps were used during the second and third stages." Two depth-jump stages were used because "a preliminary investigation ... showed that the rise in functional state achieved after one stage is unstable." "The fourth stage served as a control and served only to test performance." "The subjects were given a complete rest between stages to enhance supercompensation" (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). Fig 5.14 (verified against the page image) lays the stages out by week: resistance weeks 1-7, rest week 8, depth jumps weeks 9-15, rest week 16, depth jumps weeks 17-21, rest week 22, testing weeks 23-24. It plots Fmax (kgf), tmax (s, time to Fmax), starting strength (Ss) and explosive strength (Se). Read by eye from the image: Fmax rises from about 103 to about 110 kgf in stage 1 and reaches about 125 kgf by stage 4; tmax falls from about 0.42 s to about 0.27-0.32 s; Ss and Se both rise through stages 1-3, and Ss falls back from its stage-3 high at the stage-4 test.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' conclusion: "the plyometric method produces an additional, significant increase in the level of explosive strength that was first attained with resistance training," which shows "the use of these means in two appropriate stages: the first stage, which improves explosive strength, and the second stage, which stabilises the level of special fitness." On rest: "There was a significant increase in all the control indicators after a period of complete rest following the first and second stages. This emphasizes that rest may be used as a training means. This is not a paradox, because growth and maintenance processes take place predominantly during sleep and other forms of passive or active rest" (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). That sentence is the authors' mechanism; they cite nothing for it.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Planning a heavy-resistance block followed by a plyometric block, as in the authors' second sequencing rule ("Strong-acting plyometric methods should be done after strength exercises, but not before"; PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). Inference: plan an unloading week between blocks, as the study did, and test after it rather than on the last day of a hard block. Eric's baseline (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred, transcript): Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first. Inference: the planned rest weeks here are the opposite case to the baseline's warning against under-training: rest comes after a hard block, not in place of one.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The subjects were "qualified athletes" in a laboratory model of weightlifting preparation; no sample size, statistics or control group are given, and the "control" stage 4 is a test period, not a control group. The test was a 1RM leg extension from 90° of knee flexion, so the results are for that movement. "complete rest" between stages is not defined (passive or active, how long beyond what Fig 5.14 shows as one week). The next paragraph on the same page, about electrostimulation combined with plyometrics and heavy resistance, is a separate finding already atomized in [[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (4.2.1.6). The figure values above are approximate readings from a printed chart.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: after 7 weeks of resistance work, a rest week, then 7 and 5 weeks of depth jumps with a rest week after each, Fmax in the leg extension had risen from about 103 to about 125 kgf at the stage-4 test (Fig 5.14, PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290; values read from the image).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (ES, plyometrics and heavy resistance, same research group), [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]], [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
### case-study--junior-sprinters-short-and-long-jump-training-effects.md
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: case-study
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "5.3"
     7	topic: jump training for junior sprinters
     8	category: [sprinting, plyometrics, jump-training, special-strength]
     9	confidence: contested
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Junior Sprinters: Short Jumps Trained Stride, Long Jumps Trained Top Speed, and the Combination Was Called a Summation
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "In an experiment with junior class sprinters" three groups trained "for a period of eight months": one did mainly short jumps (repeated jumps on one and two legs, triple and quintuple standing broad jumps), one mainly long jumping exercises ("multiple jumps on one leg or from leg to leg over distances of 30-100m"), and one did both (PDF pp. 299-300 / printed pp. 288-289). The authors report: "The short jumping exercises developed primarily length and speed of the running stride, whereas the long jumping exercises largely increased maximum running speed and speed-strength endurance. The combination of short and long jumping exercises led to a summation of their separate training effects and the development of speed-strength abilities which are specific to sprinters" (PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289). Fig 5.12 (verified against the page image) plots the decrease in sprint time in seconds for each group at 30 m and 60 m from a low start (LS) and a standing start (SS), and at 100 m from a low start. Approximate bar heights read from the image (short / long / combined): 30 m LS about 0.40 / 0.08 / 0.29 s; 30 m SS about 0.07 / 0.13 / 0.20 s; 60 m LS about 0.29 / 0.22 / 0.33 s; 60 m SS about 0.08 / 0.37 / 0.43 s; 100 m LS about 0.27 / 0.50 / 1.0 s (the 100 m panel uses a 0 to 1.0 s scale). No group sizes or statistics are given.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond the outcome labels: short jumps act on stride length and stride speed, long jumps on maximum speed and speed-strength endurance, and the two "summate." Inference: the split matches the jump durations (brief standing multi-jumps vs bounding over 30-100 m), but the text does not draw that link.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Choosing jump means for sprint development: the authors' data suggest short, standing multi-jumps and long bounding series train different parts of the sprint, so a sprint-focused off-season can include both. Inference: for football, short jumps map to the start and early acceleration distances and long bounds to the longer runs, but the authors tested junior track sprinters, not football players.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book (text vs figure).** The text calls the combined effect "a summation of their separate training effects," but in Fig 5.12 the short-jump group, not the combined group, shows the largest drop at 30 m from a low start (about 0.40 vs 0.29 s). The combined group is largest at the other four distances. Read against the sum of the two single groups, the combined bar is about equal to it at 30 m SS (0.20 vs 0.07 + 0.13) and 60 m SS (0.43 vs 0.08 + 0.37), above it at 100 m LS (1.0 vs 0.27 + 0.50), and below it at 60 m LS (0.33 vs 0.29 + 0.22). So "summation" fits some distances and not others. The bar values above are read by eye from a printed chart and are approximate. The subjects were junior sprinters; the authors give no data for senior athletes.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: over 100 m from a low start, the combined jump group improved by about 1.0 s, against about 0.27 s for short jumps alone and about 0.50 s for long jumps alone (Fig 5.12, PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]] (the concurrent variant this experiment illustrates), [[claim--400m-stride-length-held-by-local-strength-endurance]], [[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]], [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas]]

     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: case-study
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "5.3"
     7	topic: sequencing strength and plyometrics in novices
     8	category: [sequencing, plyometrics, novices, special-strength, post-activation]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Novice Sequencing Experiments: Order of Strength and Speed-Strength Means Mattered Little; Depth Jumps Beat Both
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors report a set of experiments on novices in speed-strength sports (researchers named as "Purvin, Khodykin, Deniskin, Tatian and Chernousov", names checked against the page image; no dates, sample sizes or statistics are given) (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288):
    17	1. **Order across the preparatory period.** "the sequence of means in the preparatory period (beginning with strength, then speed-strength means, or vice-versa) has no real significance for novices. Consequently, the same effect can be obtained by using these means in any order."
    18	2. **Mixed sessions.** "A relatively larger effect than produced by the above-mentioned variants (with the same volume of training load) occurred in groups who used strength and speed-strength means concurrently by alternating them in mixed training sessions." The authors add that "the contrasting of stimuli in mixed workouts ... undoubtedly has a positive effect."
    19	3. **Weights then depth jumps.** One novice group did weights in stage 1 and depth jumps in stage 2, a second the reverse, a third both in both stages (not in the same workout). ### claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique.md
    14	# Too Much Heavy Strength Work Lowers Speed, Explosiveness and Technique; Speed-Strength Gains Stop After About 12-18 Weeks
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors grant that general heavy resistance exercises "enable the athlete to reach the necessary level of absolute strength, to provide general physical conditioning and to train the neuromuscular system non-specifically," but "it is undesirable to use them extensively during specialised training phases, since they can diminish speed and explosiveness. High volume strength loads used after a phase of specialised jump training can substantially reduce the existing level of explosive strength (by as much as 30%)" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291; all figures in this entry checked against the page image). Supporting reports, all cited without dates except Deniskin: Kotz, "prolonged, heavy workloads slow the contraction speed of trained muscles"; Filinov, "excessively heavy strength loads diminish the force and speed of boxers' punches"; Deniskin (1976), "prolonged use of high volume strength loads diminishes the power and speed of weightlifters, high jumpers and triple jumpers." On dose: "speed-strength and strength-speed cease to increase after a certain volume of heavy strength training has been executed. Deniskin observed this phenomenon after 18 weeks (54 workouts) of strength training. Other studies have also noted the same phenomenon after 50-60 training sessions or approximately 12 weeks of training." On technique, Siff writes (the passage names Verkhoshansky in the third person): "research by Verkhoshansky and colleagues has established that excessive maximum strength training can impair speed-strength and technical skill in boxers (Verkhoshansky, 1977). It can also lead to a deterioration of several months' duration in the technique of weightlifters and javelin throwers" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for the technique loss: "The negative influence of heavy strength training on sports technique may be due substantially to deterioration of the speed-strength qualities of the neuromuscular system," and "heavy training loads reduce one's ability to control movements, primarily of their most complex technical phases" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). For the plateau they give a dose argument only: "there are certain volumes and durations of strength training that are essential for achieving an optimum training effect. Exceeding these optimal values renders any further increase in training volume not only unproductive, but detrimental." No cellular mechanism is given.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a specialised speed or jump phase is running, keep high-volume heavy strength work out of it or small, as the authors advise. Inference: change the means of a heavy-strength emphasis before the 12-18 week mark the authors report, rather than waiting for the plateau. The authors also warn against prescribing heavy physical and technical work together for highly qualified athletes: a "literal interpretation of this concept of unified training by the concurrent prescription of physical and technical training leads to serious error," because it "contradicts the well-known need for the athlete to practise technical skills when he is fresh" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred). Inference: the authors' warning is about volume, not intensity, which fits that rule.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The 30% figure is "as much as," with no study named for it. The Kotz and Filinov reports carry no dates or data here. The 12-18 week figures are for "heavy strength training" in speed-strength athletes; the authors do not say the same plateau applies to novices or to lower-volume strength work. The section does not argue against heavy strength work in general: it calls it necessary for absolute strength and general conditioning, and criticises only extensive use during specialised phases. The authors' wider complaint (PDF p. 302) that training means are applied in a "rubber-stamp way" in which "Virtually the only factors that change are the load and overall volume" is an opinion, not a finding.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: Deniskin saw speed-strength and strength-speed stop rising after 18 weeks (54 workouts) of strength training; other studies saw it after 50-60 sessions, about 12 weeks (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]] (swimmers' explosive strength fell under concurrent endurance and strength work; agreement on interference, different cause), [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]] (stiffness and loss of explosive strength after heavy blocks), [[claim--strength-detraining-and-retention-timelines]], [[principle--sequentially-introduce-means-of-greater-training-effect]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]] (technical skill needs a rested athlete)
### claim--traditional-circuit-weight-training-gives-only-modest-mixed-benefits.md
    14	# Traditional Circuit Weight Training Gives Only Modest Mixed Benefits, Because Removing Rest Removes Heavy, Explosive and Stretching Work
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors' verdict on the "average commercial circuit": "only a moderate compromise of the reputed cardiovascular and strength conditioning benefits can be achieved by traditional circuit training" (PDF pp. 311-312 / printed pp. 300-301). Specifically: circuit weight training (CWT) "using combinations of gymnasium apparatus with fixed bicycles or mini-trampolines cannot produce cardiovascular conditioning which rivals that of running, cycling and other traditional forms"; "because CWT generally relies on the use of light weights and high repetitions, increase in strength and power is also very limited"; and "Virtually the only significant benefits of the average commercial circuit are a modest development of local muscular endurance, moderate decrease in percentage bodyfat and a mild improvement in cardiovascular fitness." "Alternation of conventional weight training on one day and endurance training on another day produces superior results to traditional circuit training in terms of improvements in strength, and cardiovascular stamina" (PDF p. 312 / printed p. 301, checked against the page image). Circuit training is dated to "R Morgan and G Adamson in 1953 at the University of Leeds" (PDF p. 311 / printed p. 300, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the rest interval. Circuit training "operates on the assumption that it can simultaneously condition you aerobically and anaerobically," and since "any rest intervals will tend to prevent the body from operating in the aerobic conditioning zone," it allows no rest beyond moving between stations (PDF p. 312 / printed p. 301). "Paradoxically, its major limitations are imposed by its very attempt to introduce aerobic conditioning into conventional weight training by eliminating rest intervals. The absence of rest periods prevents one from using heavy weights and developing strength, from holding static or resistance-assisted stretches to enhance flexibility, and from performing intensive explosive movements to improve speed" (PDF p. 313 / printed p. 302, checked against the page image). Underneath is specificity: "if one wishes to enhance strength, one has to do high intensity strength training with a minimum of prolonged aerobic training, since the latter tends to decrease strength" (PDF p. 312 / printed p. 301).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a circuit is proposed as an all-in-one strength and conditioning session, expect modest gains in each quality; for athletes who need real strength and real aerobic fitness, train them on separate days. Eric's baseline: "A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once" and priority has to be picked from what competition demands (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 115, Explicit; quoted up to the line's dash, the rest paraphrased). Inference: the authors' rejection of "simultaneous maximum conditioning" (PDF p. 312) is the same priority logic applied to strength and endurance together.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The authors cite no study for any finding in this passage ("It has been shown," "A literature review reveals"), so `supported` is a ceiling. The verdict is on "traditional" or "average commercial" circuits; the authors go on to argue that interval circuits with rest restored are far more useful (see Related), and they say "This is not to state that circuit training is of little value" (PDF p. 312 / printed p. 301). One figure on PDF p. 313 / printed p. 302 is unclear: conventional training rest of 2-4 minutes is said to be common "for few repetitions (1-3) with loads close to one's 1RM or a fairly large number of repetitions (10-15) with over 80% of one's 1RM." The image confirms the wording, but 10-15 repetitions at over 80% of 1RM is not possible for most lifters; treat that number as unclear. The note that "heavier individuals require longer recovery periods than their lighter colleagues" has no citation.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: CWT combining gym apparatus with fixed bicycles or mini-trampolines did not match the cardiovascular conditioning of running or cycling, and alternating weight-training days with endurance days beat it for both strength and stamina (PDF p. 312 / printed p. 301).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]] (Ch1, the authors' earlier CCT vs ICT verdict and fibre-type argument), [[framework--continuous-interval-and-mixed-circuit-training-classification]], [[heuristic--circuits-cannot-develop-sport-specific-strength-qualities]], [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]], [[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]]
### framework--aerobic-vs-anaerobic-circuit-parameters.md
    14	# Aerobic vs Anaerobic Circuits: Rough Guidelines for Reps, Load, Rest and Laps
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors give "rough guidelines," warning that "a considerable degree of individuality is involved and no precise figures can be quoted to be universally appropriate for everyone" (PDF p. 315 / printed p. 304, checked against the page image). Cardiovascular circuits "all fall under the category of CCT," and "A true aerobic circuit would involve the predominant use of very low resistance devices or prolonged rhythmic movements"; anaerobic circuits "may be either CCT (continuous) or ICT (interval), with the former resulting largely in muscle endurance, and variations of the latter developing strength, power, muscle endurance, speed or flexibility."

### framework--circuit-layout-variants-superset-retrophase-zigzag-detour.md
    14	# Circuit Layout Variants: A Two-Station Circuit Is a Superset, and Circuits Can Backtrack, Stagger, Detour, Pyramid or Strip
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors propose "a systems approach adapted from applied mathematics" to circuits. "The traditional approach requires one to proceed from starting station to terminal station for a certain number of sets, without backtracking, omitting stations or diverting to extra equipment"; "The more generalised approach includes the possibility of backtracking, omitting stations, altering the sequence of stations, diverting to other equipment, using different speeds of movement or time periods on each station, changing the exercise pattern at each station, and changing the types of muscle contraction at each station" (PDF p. 320 / printed p. 309, checked against the page image). The variants, each shown in a figure checked against the page images (PDF pp. 320-322 / printed pp. 309-311):
    17	- **Superset = two-station circuit.** "a circuit with two stations is exactly the same as a superset with two exercises (Fig 5.29)."
    18	- **Retrophase circuit.** "backtrack by one station for every two stations completed" (Fig 5.30); backtracking more "may cause confusion if there is a large group."
    19	- **Dual-set retrophase and sequenced supersets.** "complete two sets at each station before moving to the next station, then backtrack to complete the remaining two sets" (Fig 5.31b); or superset A and B "before going on to superset exercises C and D" (Fig 5.31a).
    20	- **Staggered or zig-zag circuit.** Lets clients "progress through portions of a circuit easily without obstructing others"; some do the inner circuit, some the outer, advanced clients "zigzag through the entire circuit," with aerobic stations in the middle of the floor (Fig 5.32).
    21	- **Detour circuit.** Clients "exit at a particular point to perform a sub-circuit" of free weights, aerobic, skill, flexibility, running, plyometric or water exercises elsewhere (Fig 5.33).
    22	- **Other variants** (PDF p. 322 / printed p. 311): repetitions to failure at each station; "pyramid circuits" in which load rises "from 40-80% of 1RM" and reps fall "e.g. from 10 to 4" with each lap; "stripping circuits" that pyramid up to "a 6RM or 10RM on each station, then progressively strip the load down," generally "about 10kg each time"; and variable-repetition or variable-interval sets. Aqualand circuits mix land and water stations (Figs 5.21-5.23, PDF pp. 317-318).
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors' stated purposes: more variety "thereby diminishing the likelihood of stagnation and boredom" (PDF p. 320 / printed p. 309), less crowding at stations (staggered circuits), and access to equipment outside the circuit (detours). For water stations they give a physical reason: "the resistance offered by water increases with the velocity of movement (actually, the square of the velocity)" and "is also directly proportional to the area of the limb pushing against the water" (PDF p. 317 / printed p. 306, checked against the page image).
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — Running a large group through limited equipment, or adding variety to a circuit block without changing its exercises. The superset equivalence is useful when writing programmes: a two-exercise superset can be planned and progressed with the same rules as a circuit. Inference: a staggered layout suits a team lift where position groups share racks, since an inner and outer loop keep groups from queuing.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — The variants are design options, not tested training methods, hence `untested`. Stripping and failure-based circuits raise fatigue; the authors say working to failure "makes it highly advisable that you have a 'spotting' partner nearby" (PDF p. 322 / printed p. 311).     15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors grant that general heavy resistance exercises "enable the athlete to reach the necessary level of absolute strength, to provide general physical conditioning and to train the neuromuscular system non-specifically," but "it is undesirable to use them extensively during specialised training phases, since they can diminish speed and explosiveness. On dose: "speed-strength and strength-speed cease to increase after a certain volume of heavy strength training has been executed. Deniskin observed this phenomenon after 18 weeks (54 workouts) of strength training. Other studies have also noted the same phenomenon after 50-60 training sessions or approximately 12 weeks of training." On technique, Siff writes (the passage names Verkhoshansky in the third person): "research by Verkhoshansky and colleagues has established that excessive maximum strength training can impair speed-strength and technical skill in boxers (Verkhoshansky, 1977).     18	**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for the technique loss: "The negative influence of heavy strength training on sports technique may be due substantially to deterioration of the speed-strength qualities of the neuromuscular system," and "heavy training loads reduce one's ability to control movements, primarily of their most complex technical phases" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). For the plateau they give a dose argument only: "there are certain volumes and durations of strength training that are essential for achieving an optimum training effect. Exceeding these optimal values renders any further increase in training volume not only unproductive, but detrimental." No cellular mechanism is given.

The authors also warn against prescribing heavy physical and technical work together for highly qualified athletes: a "literal interpretation of this concept of unified training by the concurrent prescription of physical and technical training leads to serious error," because it "contradicts the well-known need for the athlete to practise technical skills when he is fresh" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred). Inference: the authors' warning is about volume, not intensity, which fits that rule.

    14	# Traditional Circuit Weight Training Gives Only Modest Mixed Benefits, Because Removing Rest Removes Heavy, Explosive and Stretching Work

    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors warn: "The system is not without its dangers, since concentrated loading is very stressful and, besides increasing the potential for overtraining, it can decrease motor qualities such as speed-strength. After a phase of emphasis on heavy strength training, there may be an increase in muscle stiffness and a loss of explosive strength, sporting skill or speed."     14	# Across Stages: Jumps, Then Barbell Work, Then Depth Jumps; Staying on One Means Stalls or Reverses Progress
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Three "equivalent groups of jumpers of average qualification" trained "Under natural training conditions" (Verkhoshansky & Aganin 1970; Fig 5.13, verified against the page image; PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289). All used special jumping exercises in stage 1. Group 1 stayed on jumps for all three stages. Group 2 switched to barbell exercises in stage 2 and stayed there. Group 3 switched to barbell exercises in stage 2 and to depth jumps in stage 3. "The special strength training indicators displayed a clear tendency to stabilise in groups 1 and 2 after the first and second stages respectively, and in group 1, even to decrease during the third stage." The figure shows group 3's line rising through all three stages, group 2's flat in stage 3, and group 1's flattening in stage 2 and dipping in stage 3. The authors conclude: "the sequential use of means with higher, specific training effects clearly produces a positive result. At the same time, the use of the same means, even with an increase in volume, not only does not produce a positive change, but decreases the existing level of special strength fitness." From this and the novice work they draw two rules "for the sequential use of training means over a given period" (PDF pp. 300-301 / printed pp. 289-290):
    17	- "Strength exercises should be done after speed-strength exercises in training"
    18	- "Strong-acting plyometric methods should be done after strength exercises, but not before."
    19	
    20	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the sequential-means logic of 5.3: each means loses effect as the body adapts, so a stronger means must follow (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287). Fig 5.13 shows only the direction of the control indicators; it has no numerical axis. No physiological mechanism is given for why depth jumps must follow, not precede, strength work. Inference: the Deniskin (1976) laboratory study on the next page (heavy resistance, then two depth-jump stages) is the authors' supporting case for the second rule; see Related.
    21	
    22	**When to apply** — Ordering the means for jumpers or other speed-strength athletes over an off-season: general jumping first, barbell strength next, intense depth jumps last. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred). Inference: the authors' order also runs from lower to higher training effect, which fits that rule; for a football off-season this would read as general jumps and med-ball work, then a barbell-strength block, then depth jumps closer to the period where speed-strength is needed.
    23	
    24	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The same summary list ranks variants differently from the experiments reported a page earlier: it calls strength followed by speed-strength in the same session "Least effective" (PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289), while PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288 found "no statistically significant difference" between that order and its reverse in novices, and it puts mixed sessions below the best variant while PDF p. 299 says mixed sessions gave "A relatively larger effect" (see [[case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments]]). The rules come from novices and "athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 300); the authors say so in the lead-in to the list. No group sizes, statistics or units are given for Fig 5.13. Inference: the first rule reads as order over a period (stages), not within one session, since the authors introduce the rules as "for the sequential use of training means over a given period," though the same list mixes session-level and stage-level rankings; it should not be read as "lift after you jump" in a single workout, which is a separate question.     25	
    26	**Example** — The authors' own: group 3 (jumps, then barbell, then depth jumps) kept improving through stage 3, while group 1 (jumps throughout) levelled off and then declined (Fig 5.13, PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289).

    13	
    14	# Accelerating Specific Adaptation: Model the Sport, Sequence Its Demands, and Plan for Delays
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "The principle of accelerating specific adaptation emphasizes the key role of special strength training as the foundation for developing sports proficiency ... The idea is that specific adaptation should be accelerated by advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is expected to be produced by the current training regime." In practice, "the task of functional specialisation should be based on accurate modelling of all aspects of the motor activity," whose requirements "are then presented to the body in a specific sequence during the STP (Sports Training Process) in order to accelerate adaptation" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296, checked against the page image). The authors list four means of achieving it: "controlling the post-training supercompensatory phases by using the conjugate sequence method of training, by the heterochronicity principle of superimposed cycles of training the different components of fitness, by converging the partial effects of the training means, or by correctly periodised full or partial restoration after training (see 8.5)." It also "necessitates using statistical data which reflect the basic trends in the dynamics of the athlete's specific motor abilities in the given sport (see 2.2.3)" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' claim of effect: "Specialised means of strength training selected to take into account the specific movements of the given sport and the participant's existing level of fitness produce a timely and substantial increase in relative and starting strength, significantly exceeding the average indices typical of the training of that type of athlete," and "the use of complex, novel means of strength training enable highly qualified athletes to avoid the typically slow rate of increase in starting strength" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). No data or study is given for either statement on this page.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Long-range planning for an athlete with a target date: model the sport's demands, sequence them, track the athlete's abilities against norms for the sport, and keep a backup plan. The authors' contingency rule is the most directly usable part: success "depends on anticipating any conditions which may delay the subsequent course of the STP," and when fitness lags "due to unforeseen circumstances such as adaptational idiosyncrasies, illness or injury ... a contingency plan should always be available to maintain the fitness level of those systems which can still be exercised" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Eric's baseline: "Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 129, Explicit). Inference: the contingency rule (train what can still be trained during injury) is the authors' version of keeping the uninjured systems loaded during RTP.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book (two definitions).** In 5.3.3 the same term names a volume saving: "the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as much as 20%, a phenomenon referred to as the acceleration of specific adaptation (see 5.4.2)" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294). Section 5.4.2, which that sentence points to, defines it as "advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is expected" and does not mention the 20% figure (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). The two can coexist (reach the peak sooner with less volume), but the book never says so; quote whichever definition is meant. The effect claims are given without data. The "statistical data" on ability trends that the principle requires (2.2.3) may not exist for a given sport or population.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: highly qualified athletes using "complex, novel means of strength training" to avoid "the typically slow rate of increase in starting strength" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Inference: an injured lineman who cannot squat keeps upper-body and single-leg work going under the contingency rule, so the systems that can still be trained do not detrain.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--four-principles-of-special-strength-training-organisation]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]] (the 20% definition), [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[principle--converging-partial-effects-of-strength-training-means]], [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Introduce Means of Gradually Greater Training Effect, Matched to the Athlete's Current Special Fitness
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In 5.3.2, "A Sequential System of Training Means," the authors argue that the development of a specific motor ability "occurs in a specific pattern," so "it is necessary to sequentially improve the functioning of those systems and physiological mechanisms which are crucial for developing a specific motor ability" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). "Progressive functional changes in some systems act as prerequisites for improving the performance of other systems." The rule: "the means used should elicit a definite training effect, but its magnitude should correspond to the body's current level of specific fitness and increase in conjunction with the latter." Hence "the necessity ... for devising a scheme for sequentially introducing means of gradually greater training effect into training." The new means "should be novel, so as to promote a greater training effect by compelling the adaptive processes to transcend any performance plateau" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason is that earlier functional changes are prerequisites for later ones, and that "Specificity becomes more relevant to one's state of fitness as sports proficiency increases. At the same time, the role of the means used to develop trainability grows" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Novelty is given as the way past a plateau; no physiological mechanism is named. Inference: this is the same logic as the first 4.1.2 generalization (the training effect of any means diminishes as special physical fitness increases; see the taxonomy entry in Related).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When selecting means for a block, check that each one is strong enough for the athlete's current level and no stronger than needed, and plan the next, stronger means before the current one stops working. The authors name two common errors to avoid: means "selected on the spur of the moment without considering their precise training effect and often on the basis of what is currently fashionable or subjectively preferred," and "means which are highly effective during more advanced stages of training ... used inappropriately during the early stages of the yearly cycle or in the beginning stages of multi-year training." They also criticise a repertoire that "is usually extremely limited and is repeated in much the same way from year to year" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred). Inference: the authors' "gradually greater training effect" is a second axis on that spectrum: within a category, means can be ranked by strength of effect.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The authors note a limit of the evidence: "Research has investigated changing the special training means only once or twice during the period of study," while practical use needs "multiple changes" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292), so multi-change sequences are argued, not tested, here. The principle needs a ranking of means by training effect, which the authors say requires "experimental assessment" (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288); without it the ranking is a guess. "Novel" means are not the same as random variety: the authors elsewhere call random combination less effective (see Related).
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own error case: highly effective advanced means (their example category, not a named exercise) used at the start of a yearly cycle or of a young athlete's career (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Inference: depth jumps from high boxes in a freshman's first summer would be that error; the 5.3 jumper study placed them in the third stage.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the five generalizations), [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]], [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]], [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]] (5.4.4, the same principle applied), [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--plan-variation-to-avoid-restrictive-neural-patterns]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]

In practice, "the task of functional specialisation should be based on accurate modelling of all aspects of the motor activity," whose requirements "are then presented to the body in a specific sequence during the STP (Sports Training Process) in order to accelerate adaptation" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296, checked against the page image). The authors list four means of achieving it: "controlling the post-training supercompensatory phases by using the conjugate sequence method of training, by the heterochronicity principle of superimposed cycles of training the different components of fitness, by converging the partial effects of the training means, or by correctly periodised full or partial restoration after training (see 8.5)." It also "necessitates using statistical data which reflect the basic trends in the dynamics of the athlete's specific motor abilities in the given sport (see 2.2.3)" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' claim of effect: "Specialised means of strength training selected to take into account the specific movements of the given sport and the participant's existing level of fitness produce a timely and substantial increase in relative and starting strength, significantly exceeding the average indices typical of the training of that type of athlete," and "the use of complex, novel means of strength training enable highly qualified athletes to avoid the typically slow rate of increase in starting strength" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). No data or study is given for either statement on this page.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Long-range planning for an athlete with a target date: model the sport's demands, sequence them, track the athlete's abilities against norms for the sport, and keep a backup plan. The authors' contingency rule is the most directly usable part: success "depends on anticipating any conditions which may delay the subsequent course of the STP," and when fitness lags "due to unforeseen circumstances such as adaptational idiosyncrasies, illness or injury ... a contingency plan should always be available to maintain the fitness level of those systems which can still be exercised" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Eric's baseline: "Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 129, Explicit). Inference: the contingency rule (train what can still be trained during injury) is the authors' version of keeping the uninjured systems loaded during RTP.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book (two definitions).** In 5.3.3 the same term names a volume saving: "the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as much as 20%, a phenomenon referred to as the acceleration of specific adaptation (see 5.4.2)" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294). Section 5.4.2, which that sentence points to, defines it as "advancing the stage when maximum sports proficiency is expected" and does not mention the 20% figure (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). The two can coexist (reach the peak sooner with less volume), but the book never says so; quote whichever definition is meant. The effect claims are given without data. The "statistical data" on ability trends that the principle requires (2.2.3) may not exist for a given sport or population.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: highly qualified athletes using "complex, novel means of strength training" to avoid "the typically slow rate of increase in starting strength" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296). Inference: an injured lineman who cannot squat keeps upper-body and single-leg work going under the contingency rule, so the systems that can still be trained do not detrain.

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Introduce Means of Gradually Greater Training Effect, Matched to the Athlete's Current Special Fitness
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In 5.3.2, "A Sequential System of Training Means," the authors argue that the development of a specific motor ability "occurs in a specific pattern," so "it is necessary to sequentially improve the functioning of those systems and physiological mechanisms which are crucial for developing a specific motor ability" (PDF p. 302 / printed p. 291). "Progressive functional changes in some systems act as prerequisites for improving the performance of other systems." The rule: "the means used should elicit a definite training effect, but its magnitude should correspond to the body's current level of specific fitness and increase in conjunction with the latter." Hence "the necessity ... for devising a scheme for sequentially introducing means of gradually greater training effect into training." The new means "should be novel, so as to promote a greater training effect by compelling the adaptive processes to transcend any performance plateau" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason is that earlier functional changes are prerequisites for later ones, and that "Specificity becomes more relevant to one's state of fitness as sports proficiency increases. At the same time, the role of the means used to develop trainability grows" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Novelty is given as the way past a plateau; no physiological mechanism is named. Inference: this is the same logic as the first 4.1.2 generalization (the training effect of any means diminishes as special physical fitness increases; see the taxonomy entry in Related).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When selecting means for a block, check that each one is strong enough for the athlete's current level and no stronger than needed, and plan the next, stronger means before the current one stops working. The authors name two common errors to avoid: means "selected on the spur of the moment without considering their precise training effect and often on the basis of what is currently fashionable or subjectively preferred," and "means which are highly effective during more advanced stages of training ... used inappropriately during the early stages of the yearly cycle or in the beginning stages of multi-year training." They also criticise a repertoire that "is usually extremely limited and is repeated in much the same way from year to year" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred). Inference: the authors' "gradually greater training effect" is a second axis on that spectrum: within a category, means can be ranked by strength of effect.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The authors note a limit of the evidence: "Research has investigated changing the special training means only once or twice during the period of study," while practical use needs "multiple changes" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292), so multi-change sequences are argued, not tested, here. The principle needs a ranking of means by training effect, which the authors say requires "experimental assessment" (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288); without it the ranking is a guess. "Novel" means are not the same as random variety: the authors elsewhere call random combination less effective (see Related).
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own error case: highly effective advanced means (their example category, not a named exercise) used at the start of a yearly cycle or of a young athlete's career (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). Inference: depth jumps from high boxes in a freshman's first summer would be that error; the 5.3 jumper study placed them in the third stage.

The plyometric method of developing explosive strength and reactive ability solves to a significant degree the 
problem of economising training, since it ensures that a high level of special conditioning is attained in the 
minimum time. Thus, a comparative experiment revealed that a group of track-and-field jumpers executing 
primarily depth-jumps (all of them did 475 jumps) over a 12 week period in the preparation phase showed greater 
improvement in reactive ability than the group which trained with traditional methods and executed 1472 general 
push-offs (squats, jumping and hopping with a barbell weighing 90-95%, 70-80% and 30-40% of 1RM) and lifted 
i total volume of 93 tons! Carefully periodised training programmes which combine resistance exercises with 
plyomctrics can develop explosive strength even more effectively than plyometrics alone, provided the resistance 
movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions.
The use of many repetitions and sets of plyometric drills in an attempt to facilitate adaptation to cope with 
exhaustive bouts of stretch-shortening activities such as rebounding in basketball is not supported by research 
(Nicol et al, 1997). Instead any improvement in such situations is better mediated by the use of training to 
enhance movement efficiency. This is a very important point which concerns all explosive and ballistic activities:

have resulted from the separate non-systematic use of these same means, even at increased volume. Experimental 
assessment of the cumulative effects of different variations of the combination of means is necessary for applying 
the complex system of special strength training means.
A number of researchers, including Purvin, FChodykin, Dcniskin, Tatian and Chemousov have studied the 
systematic use of special strength means in speed-strength sports. They have established that the sequence of 
means in the preparatory period (beginning with strength, then speed-strength means, or vice-versa) has no real 
significance for novices. Consequently, the same effect can be obtained by using these means in any order.
A relatively larger effect than produced by the above-mentioned variants (with the same volume of training 
load) occun-ed in groups who used strength and speed-strength means concurrently by alternating them in mixed 
training sessions. This alternation sequence creates the optimal conditions for functional adaptation. This docs 
not ignore the fact that this training regime, with a rest interval between sessions on the same day, also produces a 
positive response of the after-effect phenomenon by use of the strength and speed-strength exercises. On the 
whole, this elicitcd more intense and more stable adaptation. It should be noted that the contrasting of stimuli in 
mixed workouts by alternating training means which are primarily of a strength and speed-strength character 
undoubtedly has a positive effect.
In another experiment one group of novice athletes used weights exercises in the first stage of training and 
plyometric depth jumps in the next stage. A second group did the same exercises in reverse order and a third 
group did these same exercises together in both stages, although not in the same workout. It was established that 
the first variant was more effective for developing speed-strength. The concurrent use of exercises (the third 
variant) caused significant improvement in speed-strength in the first stage, but the rate of improvement in speed- 
strength decreased noticeably in the second stage, due to monotonous repetition. The second variant (reversed use 
of these same means) produced significant improvement after the first stage due to the larger training effect of the 
plyometric method. However, the acquired speed-strength qualities were lowest at the end o f the second stage.
Another experiment studied the question of whether the execution of speed-strength exercises in one workout 
against the background of the positive after-effect produced by previous tonic strength work influences the 
effectiveness of speed-strength preparation of novices. One group of athletes executed exercises in this sequence 
(i.e. strength, then speed-strcngth work) during the fundamental stage of their workouts, while another group did 
the reverse. The pauses between exercises were increased slightly to minimise the influence of the positive after­
effect of the preceding work on the subsequent work. A third group executed depth jumps. The presence of this 
group in the experiment served two purposes: firstly, to study the effectiveness of plyometrics and secondly, to 
compare this effect with the results obtained with a complcx of less effective means. There was no statistically 
significant difference in speed-strength of the subjects in the first two groups. The largest increase in all the 
parameters of the control movement was discovered in the third group.
Thus, an increase in the training effect of speed-strength exercises performed against the background of the 
positive after-effect of strength work has not been corroborated in the training of novices. In this experiment, the 
means with a higher training effect (i.e. dcpth-jumps) produced significantly larger improvement in speed-strength 
fitness for a smaller volume of training. In explaining these results, one should take into account that any training 
influence will leave significant traces in an untrained person. The body is unable to react selectively to a chiefly 
strength or speed-strength means in one workout. In addition, the period over which the traces of the training 
stimulus are maintained is apparently longer than the duration of the after-effect of prior tonic work. Within one 
workout, the traccs of all the training tasks arc summed, which results in the same effect, despite these tasks being 
done in succession.
These findings should not be considered to disprove in general the appropriateness of using a complex of 
means in training, which exploits the positive after-effect of preceding strength work to enhance the training effect 
of the subsequent speed-strength and speed work. Since the experiment was conducted on a group of novice 
athletes, it is very likely that their lower level of special fitness excluded the possibility for exploiting this 
phenomenon adequately. A well-trained athlete can expect the preceding strength work to have a positive effect 
on the training effect of speed-strength and speed work in a training programme. However, the validity of this 
hypothesis can be established conclusively only by careful experimentation.
In an experiment with junior class sprinters the specific effect of short jumping exercises and the systematic 
use of combinations of these exercises was investigated. The jumping exercises involved variations of repeated 
jumps on one and two legs, as well as variations of triple and quintuple standing broad jumps and long jumping 
exercises (multiple jumps on one leg or from leg to leg over distances of 30- 100m). One group of sprinters 
executed mainly short jumps, a second group did mainly long jumping exercises and a third group did both fora
288

######## PDF 300

period of eight months (see Fig 5.12). The short jumping exercises developed primarily length and speed of the 
running stride, whereas the long jumping exercises largely increased maximum running speed and speed-strength 
endurance. The combination of short and long jumping cxerciscs led to a summation of their separate training 
effects and the development of speed-strength abilities which arc specific to sprinters.
Figure 5.12 Decrease in sprint times for three groups of athletes over various distances after 8 months of training. LS = low start, SS 
= standing start. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
Under natural training conditions, three equivalent groups of jumpers of average qualification were used to 
compare the effectiveness of different systems of strength training (Fig 5.13). All of the groups used special 
jumping exercises in the first stage of the preparation period. Groups 2 and 3 switched to barbell exercises in the 
second stage, while group 1 continued to do the jumping exercises. Group 3 began to use depth-jumps in the third 
sage while group 1 continued to do the jumping exercises and group 2 did the barbell exercises.
The special strength training indicators displayed a clear tendency to stabilise in groups 1 and 2 after the first 
and second stages respectively, and in group 1, even to decrease during the third stage. Thus, the sequential use of 
means with higher, specific training effects dearly produces a positive result. At the same time, the use of the 
same means, even with an increase in volume, not only does not produce a positive change, but decreases the 
existing level of special strength fitness (Verkhoshansky & Aganin, 1970).
Research with novices and athletes of average qualification leads us to make the following conclusions about 
the effectiveness of the variants studied for these athletes:
• The best results are obtained by consistently using those combinations or complexes o f means which 
produce the optimal training effect (e.g. as shown in Fig 5.13)
• A slightly smaller effect is obtained by the concurrent use of strength and speed-strength means in one 
training session or their sequential use in successive sessions
• Least effective is the sequence of strength followed by speed-strength means during the same session.
Figure 5.13 Dynamics of the control indicators for the three groups using different combinations of training methods (see the text). 
(Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
Tk following principles for the sequential use of training means over a given period emerge:

explosive strength. Only depth-jumps were used during the sccond and third stages. The necessity for having two 
such stages was dictated by the results of a preliminary investigation which showed that the rise in functional

# Deniskin (1976): A Resistance Stage, Then Two Depth-Jump Stages, With Complete Rest Between Them

**What it is** — "qualified athletes modelled different variants of weightlifting pre-competition training under laboratory conditions (Deniskin, 1976)." The test movement was "A leg extension movement involving the lifting of a 1RM ... starting with an initial knee angle of 90°." Stage 1 was "intensive work with resistance, the purpose of which was to increase explosive strength." "Only depth-jumps were used during the second and third stages." Two depth-jump stages were used because "a preliminary investigation ... showed that the rise in functional state achieved after one stage is unstable." "The fourth stage served as a control and served only to test performance." "The subjects were given a complete rest between stages to enhance supercompensation" (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). Fig 5.14 (verified against the page image) lays the stages out by week: resistance weeks 1-7, rest week 8, depth jumps weeks 9-15, rest week 16, depth jumps weeks 17-21, rest week 22, testing weeks 23-24. It plots Fmax (kgf), tmax (s, time to Fmax), starting strength (Ss) and explosive strength (Se). Read by eye from the image: Fmax rises from about 103 to about 110 kgf in stage 1 and reaches about 125 kgf by stage 4; tmax falls from about 0.42 s to about 0.27-0.32 s; Ss and Se both rise through stages 1-3, and Ss falls back from its stage-3 high at the stage-4 test.

**Why it works** — The authors' conclusion: "the plyometric method produces an additional, significant increase in the level of explosive strength that was first attained with resistance training," which shows "the use of these means in two appropriate stages: the first stage, which improves explosive strength, and the second stage, which stabilises the level of special fitness." On rest: "There was a significant increase in all the control indicators after a period of complete rest following the first and second stages. This emphasizes that rest may be used as a training means. This is not a paradox, because growth and maintenance processes take place predominantly during sleep and other forms of passive or active rest" (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). That sentence is the authors' mechanism; they cite nothing for it.

**When to apply** — Planning a heavy-resistance block followed by a plyometric block, as in the authors' second sequencing rule ("Strong-acting plyometric methods should be done after strength exercises, but not before"; PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). Inference: plan an unloading week between blocks, as the study did, and test after it rather than on the last day of a hard block. Eric's baseline (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred, transcript): Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first. Inference: the planned rest weeks here are the opposite case to the baseline's warning against under-training: rest comes after a hard block, not in place of one.

**When NOT to apply** — The subjects were "qualified athletes" in a laboratory model of weightlifting preparation; no sample size, statistics or control group are given, and the "control" stage 4 is a test period, not a control group. The test was a 1RM leg extension from 90° of knee flexion, so the results are for that movement. "complete rest" between stages is not defined (passive or active, how long beyond what Fig 5.14 shows as one week). The next paragraph on the same page, about electrostimulation combined with plyometrics and heavy resistance, is a separate finding already atomized in [[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (4.2.1.6). The figure values above are approximate readings from a printed chart.

**Example** — The authors' own: after 7 weeks of resistance work, a rest week, then 7 and 5 weeks of depth jumps with a rest week after each, Fmax in the leg extension had risen from about 103 to about 125 kgf at the stage-4 test (Fig 5.14, PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290; values read from the image).

**Related** — [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[heuristic--electrostimulation-sequencing-dosage-and-safety-practicalities]] (ES, plyometrics and heavy resistance, same research group), [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]], [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]

This emphasizes that rest may be used as a training means. Stage 1 was "intensive work with resistance, the purpose of which was to increase explosive strength." "Only depth-jumps were used during the second and third stages." Two depth-jump stages were used because "a preliminary investigation ... showed that the rise in functional state achieved after one stage is unstable." "The fourth stage served as a control and served only to test performance." "The subjects were given a complete rest between stages to enhance supercompensation" (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). lines: # Deniskin (1976): A Resistance Stage, Then Two Depth-Jump Stages, With Complete Rest Between Them

-**What it is** — "qualified athletes modelled different variants of weightlifting pre-competition training under laboratory conditions (Deniskin, 1976)." The test movement was "A leg extension movement involving the lifting of a 1RM ... starting with an initial knee angle of 90°." Stage 1 was "intensive work with resistance, the purpose of which was to increase explosive strength." "Only depth-jumps were used during the second and third stages." Two depth-jump stages were used because "a preliminary investigation ... showed that the rise in functional state achieved after one stage is unstable." "The fourth stage served as a control and served only to test performance." "The subjects were given a complete rest between stages to enhance supercompensation" (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). Fig 5.14 (verified against the page image) lays the stages out by week: resistance weeks 1-7, rest week 8, depth jumps weeks 9-15, rest week 16, depth jumps weeks 17-21, rest week 22, testing weeks 23-24. It plots Fmax (kgf), tmax (s, time to Fmax), starting strength (Ss) and explosive strength (Se). Read by eye from the image: Fmax rises from about 103 to about 110 kgf in stage 1 and reaches about 125 kgf by stage 4; tmax falls from about 0.42 s to about 0.27-0.32 s. Ss and Se jump after each rest week (weeks 8 and 16): Ss from about 500 at the end of stage 1 to about 565 at the start of stage 2, and from about 610 to about 665 into stage 3; Se from about 280 to about 340, and from about 400 to about 430. Both are at their highest early in stage 3 (Ss peaks at about 685 in week 19; Se is highest at about 430 in week 17). Both then decline through stage 3 (Ss to about 625, Se to about 380 by week 21) and sit below that peak at the stage-4 test (Ss about 580-625, Se about 375-400). Ss and Se values are read by eye from the image; the axis carries numbers but no unit.

**Why it works** — The authors' conclusion: "the plyometric method produces an additional, significant increase in the level of explosive strength that was first attained with resistance training," which shows "the use of these means in two appropriate stages: the first stage, which improves explosive strength, and the second stage, which stabilises the level of special fitness." On rest: "There was a significant increase in all the control indicators after a period of complete rest following the first and second stages. This emphasizes that rest may be used as a training means. This is not a paradox, because growth and maintenance processes take place predominantly during sleep and other forms of passive or active rest" (PDF p. 301 / printed p. 290). That sentence is the authors' mechanism; they cite nothing for it.

**When to apply** — Choosing jump means for sprint development: the authors' data suggest short, standing multi-jumps and long bounding series train different parts of the sprint, so a sprint-focused off-season can include both. Inference: for football, short jumps map to the start and early acceleration distances and long bounds to the longer runs, but the authors tested junior track sprinters, not football players.

-**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book (text vs figure).** The text calls the combined effect "a summation of their separate training effects," but in Fig 5.12 the short-jump group, not the combined group, shows the largest drop at 30 m LS (about 0.39 vs 0.25 s). The combined group is largest at the other four distances. Against the sum of the two single groups, the combined bar is below it at 30 m SS (0.19 vs 0.22) and 60 m LS (0.29 vs 0.47), about equal at 60 m SS (0.42 vs 0.45), and above it only at 100 m LS (1.0 vs 0.77). Across stages, their data favour heavy resistance first and depth jumps after. The authors limit the within-workout finding to novices: "it is very likely that their lower level of special fitness excluded the possibility for exploiting this phenomenon adequately. A well-trained athlete can expect the preceding strength work to have a positive effect ... However, the validity of this hypothesis can be established conclusively only by careful experimentation" (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288). -**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The authors' own summary on the next page reads: "A slightly smaller effect is obtained by the concurrent use of strength and speed-strength means in one training session or their sequential use in successive sessions" and "Least effective is the sequence of strength followed by speed-strength means during the same session" (PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289). The second sentence ranks strength-then-speed-strength in one session last, while PDF p. 299 found "no statistically significant difference" between that order and its reverse. The PDF p. 299 statement that order "has no real significance for novices" also sits uneasily with experiment 3 on the same page, where weights-then-depth-jumps beat the reverse order in novices. The book also states, in 5.2.4, that resistance plus plyometrics works best "provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277), which sits against experiment 4's null within-session result in novices. The first summary sentence, that mixed or successive-session use gives "A slightly smaller effect", compares them with the best variant (the Fig 5.13 complexes), while PDF p. 299 compares mixed sessions with the two order variants, so those two statements do not conflict.
